question: A team stores drivers with a B-tree index on `(lat, lon)` and runs a bounding-box query around each rider. It is fast in one city and slow after the service goes global. Why?
options: B-trees cannot store negative numbers, so longitudes west of Greenwich are skipped
The index seeks only on the `lat` range, so each query walks every driver in a latitude band around the planet and filters `lon` afterwards
Bounding boxes require a full table lock on every read
The query returns drivers from the wrong hemisphere because of floating-point rounding
explanation: A composite B-tree uses the first column for the range seek; the second column is filtered row by row. A cell id turns the query into a few exact-match lookups whose cost does not grow with drivers elsewhere.

question: Why did H3 choose hexagons rather than squares for its cells?
options: Hexagons tile a sphere perfectly with no exceptions
Hexagon ids are shorter strings than square ids
All six neighbors of a hexagon are at the same distance from its center, so rings of cells approximate a circle and movement between cells is smoother to analyze
Squares cannot be given integer identifiers
explanation: A square has edge neighbors and corner neighbors at two different distances. Hexagons have one neighbor distance; they still need 12 pentagons per resolution because a sphere cannot be tiled with hexagons only.

question: Dispatch works on fine H3 cells, but the pricing team wants supply and demand per neighborhood. What is the H3 way to get coarser counts?
options: Map each fine cell id to its parent at a coarser resolution, a cheap bitwise truncation, and aggregate the counts by parent id
Store every location a second time with a bounding box per neighborhood
Re-run the geometry from the raw coordinates with a different cell shape
Average the latitudes of all cells in the city
explanation: H3 is hierarchical: each resolution has cells about one seventh the area of the coarser one, and the parent id is found by truncating bits of the 64-bit index, so aggregation is a group-by on a derived key.

question: Location updates flow through a Kafka topic into the driver index. After a busy evening, drivers show up in several cells at once and cells near the highway report too much supply. What is the most likely bug?
options: The topic has too many partitions
The consumer adds the driver to the new cell but never removes them from the previous one
The cell size is too large
Kafka delivered the messages out of order across different drivers
explanation: An update must be a move: look up the driver's current cell, leave it, then join the new one. Without the driver → cell map every cell a driver crossed keeps a stale entry and inflates the supply counts.

question: In Uber's Domain-Oriented Microservice Architecture (DOMA), what does a domain gateway provide?
options: A load balancer that picks the least busy service with two random choices
A shared database that every domain writes to
A rule that every service must be written in the same language
A single entry point into a domain, so callers depend on one interface while the services behind it can change
explanation: Gateways hide the services, tables and pipelines inside a domain; callers take one dependency instead of many, which is what lets a domain be rewritten behind its gateway without migrating every caller.

question: A stadium empties and thousands of riders open the app in the same few cells. Which design choice keeps the driver index from becoming a hot spot?
options: Switch every query to a global bounding-box scan
Disable the k-ring and only read the rider's own cell
Cache each cell's driver list with a short TTL and coalesce concurrent reads of the same cell into one load
Turn off caching for those cells so every rider reads the freshest driver list from the index
explanation: Cell ids are ordinary keys, so hot-key defenses apply: request coalescing turns thousands of concurrent misses on the same cell into one load, and the short TTL keeps the list fresh. Resharding does not help: every rider asks for the same few keys, and each key lives on one shard.
